<reason>Both sides built genuine, textured cases with sustained clash rather than parallel monologues. B's opening and first rebuttal landed a real blow by turning the Omicron/South Africa case into evidence that exposure invites punishment WHO cannot restrain, and B's "cameras and flight-trackers" point against A's nuclear-inspection separability model was a sharp, concrete challenge that A never fully answered on its own terms. But A's repeated move of flipping that same South Africa example — sovereignty had full messaging control there and still failed to prevent punishment — was the more decisive turn in the debate, because it neutralized B's central selling point (that sovereign discretion buys protection) while leaving intact A's own strongest asymmetry: sovereignty additionally produces the catastrophic delay costs of SARS and Wuhan that verification access would remove. B's late pivot to "discretion over when to risk exposure" and "defensive freeze by willing states" were reasonable adaptations, but they shifted the goalpost rather than squarely closing the gap A opened, and B's strongest optics-based rebuttal against separability faded from the closing rather than being pressed home. A's closing crystallized the comparison more cleanly: both regimes fail to stop punishment, only one guarantees delay. That made A's case marginally easier to decide on the terms the debate itself established.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's repeated use of the Omicron/South Africa example (A2.1, A4.3, A5.1) to show that sovereign messaging control did not even deliver its promised benefit of avoiding punishment, undercutting B's core justification for preserving national control, versus B's camera/flight-tracker rebuttal (B4.3) exposing the fragility of A's verification/announcement separability claim.</best_rebuttal>
